aiOverview.content: Traveling internationally may increase your risk of encountering diseases that are rare in the United States, making it essential to ensure you are up to date with both routine and travel-specific vaccinations. The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) recommends visiting a travel medicine specialist or your healthcare provider 4–6 weeks before departure to discuss your itinerary and receive tailored advice. Key Considerations for 2026 Travel Polio Alert (March 2026): The CDC has issued a Level 2 travel advisory for over 30 countries due to polio detections, advising travelers to ensure their polio vaccinations are up to date. Measles: Cases are rising globally; travelers should be fully vaccinated against measles. Yellow Fever: Specific countries in Africa and South America require proof of vaccination (Yellow Card), which is only valid 10 days after administration. Last-Minute Travel: Even if departing soon, vaccinations still provide value and may be available on an accelerated schedule. Recommended Travel Vaccinations (By Type) 1. Routine Vaccinations (Ensure these are current) COVID-19 Measles-mumps-rubella (MMR) Diphtheria-tetanus-pertussis (Tdap) Varicella (Chickenpox) Influenza (Flu) Polio 2. Common Travel-Specific Vaccinations Hepatitis A: Recommended for most travelers going to countries with poor food/water sanitation. Typhoid: Recommended for travelers visiting South Asia (India, Pakistan, Bangladesh) or other areas with high risk. Yellow Fever: Required for entry into certain countries in Africa and South America. Japanese Encephalitis: Recommended for long-term travel (≥1 month) or rural visits in Asia. Meningococcal Disease: Recommended for the African meningitis belt and required for Hajj/Umrah travelers to Saudi Arabia. Rabies: Recommended for travelers visiting areas where dog bites are common, or for long-stay/rural travelers. Tick-borne Encephalitis (TBE): Recommended for travelers going to TBE-endemic areas in Europe or Asia who plan outdoor activities. Timeline for Vaccination 4–6 Weeks Out: Initial consultation with a doctor. 10 Days Prior: Minimum time needed for yellow fever vaccine to become effective for entry requirements. < 2 Weeks: Some vaccines (like Hepatitis A) can still offer protection, and some can be given on an accelerated schedule. Where to Get Vaccinated Travel Medicine Clinics: Often located within major hospital systems or private, specialized clinics. Local Health Departments: Frequently offer travel immunizations. Pharmacies: Many national pharmacy chains (e.g., CVS MinuteClinic) offer consultations and vaccinations. For customized recommendations, use the CDC Travelers' Health destination tool.
